title: 2025 Supervisory Stress Test Methodology
summary: The Federal Reserve Board published its 2025 Supervisory Stress Test Methodology in June 2025, providing detailed descriptions of the models used to assess how large banks perform under hypothetical severe economic conditions. The methodology document covers pre-provision net revenue models, loan loss projections across corporate, commercial real estate, residential mortgage, and credit card portfolios, and the calculation of regulatory capital ratios under stress scenarios.
key_points: The Fed conducts annual supervisory stress tests as required by the Dodd-Frank Act for firms with $100 billion or more in assets (BHCs, SLHCs, and IHCs of foreign banks).
The stress test framework projects pre-tax net income, balance sheet changes, and resulting regulatory capital ratios under hypothetical economic scenarios.
Loan loss models cover four major categories: corporate loans, commercial real estate (CRE) loans, domestic first-lien residential mortgages, and domestic credit cards.
The methodology includes model risk management policies, governance frameworks, and validation procedures for supervisory models.

As part of the annual cycle, the Fed publishes four documents: Stress Test Scenarios (mid-February), Supervisory Stress Test Methodology, Federal Reserve Stress Test Results (end of Q2), and Large Bank Capital Requirements (Q3).
The document is part of the Fed's transparency efforts to improve public understanding of how stress test models estimate bank resilience.
why_it_matters: Bank investors and financial system monitors use Fed stress test methodology to understand how capital requirements are derived. Changes to loss rate models or assumptions can affect estimated capital depletion under stress, influencing dividend capacity, buyback expectations, and risk weights for bank stocks. The methodology is the technical foundation for regulatory capital requirements that bind large banks.
macro_context: The 2025 Stress Test Methodology document is published in June, before the actual stress test results (typically end of Q2) and capital requirements (Q3). While the methodology itself is not a market-moving event, the resulting stress test outputs later in the year can influence bank stock valuations, capital requirement expectations, and dividend/buyback capacity for large bank equities.
market_structure_context: Fed stress test methodology determines capital buffer requirements for large banks ($100B+). These capital requirements affect how much leverage banks can carry, which indirectly influences their market-making capacity, securities lending activity, and ability to provide credit during stress periods. The methodology's loan loss models (corporate, CRE, mortgage, credit card) project how bank balance sheets would be impacted in a severe recession.
